item.text:
Below is a text-only issue list for counsel’s review before the October 15 markup. **These are potential exemptions, interpretive disputes, and implementation defects—not assured lawful ways to continue operating.** Several depend on agency interpretation or judicial resolution; a complete assessment would also require applicable background law.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Strict compute threshold.** The definition covers training using *greater than* \(10^{26}\) operations, leaving a run at exactly that threshold outside the compute-based trigger. Such a system could still be covered under § 2(1)(B).

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” is undefined.** The text does not say whether interrupted training, successive checkpoints, continued pretraining, or separate training stages constitute one run. This leaves uncertainty over whether their compute must be aggregated.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—No aggregation across related models.** The bill does not expressly combine compute used to train separate models, ensembles, or components of a larger system. A system assembled from individually below-threshold models might escape the compute trigger, although the capability trigger remains available.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** There is no methodology for counting operations, including sparse computation, mixed precision, recomputation, or unsuccessful training work. Different accounting conventions could produce different coverage determinations.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Non-integer/non-floating-point computation.** The definition expressly counts integer and floating-point operations but does not address analog or other computational methods. Whether those methods count by equivalence is unresolved.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Training versus other computation.** The text does not specify how to treat inference-time computation, search, synthetic-data generation, or other work supporting training. Large amounts of capability-producing computation may fall outside the stated training-run metric.

7. **§ 2(1)—“Model” and “system” differ without explanation.** Paragraph (A) covers a model, while paragraph (B) covers a system, and neither term is defined. The treatment of agents, tool-connected models, ensembles, and downstream integrations is consequently uncertain.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines which Secretary makes capability determinations. Commerce is a plausible contextual inference, but § 6 expressly assigns a separate role to the Secretary of State.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Capability standards are indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, reference populations, or measurement rules. Coverage could change materially depending on the chosen tests and human comparison group.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage appears to require an affirmative determination.** Unlike the compute trigger, the capability trigger applies to a system “that the Secretary determines” meets the standard. The text does not establish whether coverage can precede that determination or reach earlier conduct.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure.** There are no specified procedures for notice, testing, evidence, timing, reconsideration, or appeals. Generally applicable administrative law may supply some protections, but the bill itself does not establish a workable designation process.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—Version and configuration uncertainty.** The bill does not say whether a determination covers only the evaluated version or also derivatives, updates, differently configured deployments, and related models. That creates uncertainty about both the reach and durability of a designation.

13. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits noncitizen residents and expressly names only corporations organized under state law, not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or other entities. Those omissions matter principally outside the United States, because § 3(a) separately covers any person within the country.

14. **§ 2(2)—Non-state incorporation is unaddressed.** Corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law are not expressly included. Whether “State” encompasses any of these jurisdictions would require interpretation.

15. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and attribution.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not expressly a U.S. person merely because a U.S. corporation owns it. The bill lacks specific ownership, control, or attribution provisions, although indirect participation and generally applicable liability doctrines could still reach U.S. actors.

16. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** There are no performance specifications or rules for counting chiplets, accelerator packages, or multifunction processors. Facility coverage therefore rests on an undefined technological category.

17. **§ 2(3)—Strict facility threshold and no aggregation.** A facility containing exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is outside the definition, and the bill does not aggregate separate data centers. This limits registry coverage, not the independent prohibition in § 3.

18. **§ 2(3)—Facility boundaries and counting dates are unspecified.** The text does not define whether a campus, building, leased space, or distributed cluster is one data center, or when chip inventory is measured. Treatment of stored, inactive, leased, and temporarily installed chips is also unclear.

### Prohibition and exemptions

19. **§ 3(a)—Prohibited activities are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” have no statutory definitions. Research, fine-tuning, distributing weights, hosting, making API access available, and ordinary use could fall on different sides of those terms.

20. **§ 3(a)—Coverage during development is unclear.** A model may not become covered until training exceeds the threshold or a capability determination occurs. The bill does not clearly identify when preparatory or ongoing development becomes unlawful.

21. **§ 3(a)—Location of remote activity is unresolved.** The text does not explain where training, development, or deployment occurs when personnel, servers, and users are in different countries. This particularly affects foreign persons operating overseas infrastructure accessed from the United States.

22. **§ 3(a)—Supporting activities are not expressly prohibited.** Providing compute, financing, supplying chips, or transferring technology is not separately listed. Such conduct might constitute development or support liability under other law, but the bill does not clearly establish that reach.

23. **§ 3(a)—Possession and dismantling are unaddressed.** The bill does not expressly require deletion of weights, surrender of systems, shutdown of facilities, or prohibit mere possession. Continuing deployment may be unlawful, but retaining an inactive system is not expressly forbidden.

24. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts systems, not merely ongoing training.** The exemption removes qualifying pre-enactment systems from all of § 3(a), including its development and deployment prohibitions. It therefore appears substantially broader than permission to finish an existing training run.

25. **§ 3(b)—No grandfathering completion deadline.** A system whose training began before enactment has no specified deadline for completing training or ending operation. The exemption could persist for the Act’s entire duration.

26. **§ 3(b)—“Training began” has no substantive minimum.** The text does not specify the amount or character of training needed to establish a pre-enactment start. A dispute could arise over whether a preliminary or minimal training step suffices.

27. **§ 3(b)—System continuity and derivatives are unresolved.** The exemption does not explain when additional training, architectural changes, new versions, or derivative models become a different system. This makes the scope of grandfathered future development uncertain.

28. **§§ 3(b), 8—Grandfathering and effective dates do not align.** Systems begun during the 180-day period after enactment are not grandfathered, even though the Act has not yet taken effect. Their later training, development, or deployment would therefore face a different treatment from pre-enactment systems.

29. **§ 3(c)—Safety-evaluation exemption is broad.** The exemption is not limited to specified evaluators, approved protocols, controlled environments, or particular activities. Its wording could encompass otherwise prohibited training, development, or deployment undertaken for safety evaluation.

30. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose. Activities serving both evaluation and commercial development create a significant exemption dispute, though merely relabeling commercial work would not necessarily qualify.

31. **§ 3(c)—No evaluation safeguards or verification process.** There are no express limits on duration, scale, access, or downstream use, and no approval or reporting requirement. The bill also does not specify how an asserted evaluation purpose must be substantiated.

### Registry and enforcement

32. **§ 4(a)—No registration deadline or updating rules.** Operators must register, but the bill gives no deadline after effectiveness or after a facility crosses the threshold. It also lacks rules for ownership changes, inventory changes, and deregistration.

33. **§ 4(a)—“Operator” and geographic scope are unclear.** Responsibilities are uncertain for landlords, cloud providers, tenants, and jointly operated facilities. Unlike § 3, § 4 does not expressly state its territorial or extraterritorial reach.

34. **§ 4(b)—Reporting standards are unspecified.** “Describing the computing workloads” establishes no required detail, accounting methodology, report format, or first reporting date. Operator certification is required, but the text provides no verification or audit mechanism.

35. **§ 4(b)—Reports are tied to registered operators.** The reporting duty expressly applies to “each registered operator,” leaving uncertainty about reporting obligations before registration occurs. Failure to register still violates § 4(a), but the wording creates an avoidable enforcement gap.

36. **§§ 4, 5—No express penalties for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3, not failures to register or report under § 4. Other laws may address false statements or other misconduct, but this Act supplies no dedicated registry penalty.

37. **§§ 2, 4, 5—Limited express investigative machinery.** The bill does not expressly authorize inspections, compulsory testing, subpoenas, or mandatory model-level compute records. Existing governmental authority might fill some gaps, but registry reports alone may not establish coverage or violations.

38. **§ 5—Enforcement responsibility and procedure are unspecified.** The bill does not identify who assesses civil penalties or provide an administrative enforcement process. It also does not expressly authorize injunctions or shutdown orders, leaving their availability dependent on other law.

39. **§ 5(a)—Penalty unit is ambiguous.** “For each day on which the violation occurs” does not clearly establish whether separate systems or separate prohibited acts generate separate daily penalties. It also leaves uncertainty about the duration of a continuing development or deployment violation.

40. **§ 5(a)—No express civil culpability standard.** The provision does not state whether civil liability requires knowledge, negligence, or neither. That matters where compute totals or capability coverage are uncertain.

41. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” creates a separate proof issue.** Criminal liability requires willfulness, but the text does not specify what knowledge that entails, including knowledge of coverage or illegality. Ambiguous definitions and exemptions could complicate proving the required mental state.

42. **§§ 5(a), 8—Civil penalties and effectiveness conflict.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness by 180 days. The text does not clearly resolve whether any pre-effective-date conduct is punishable; constitutional and statutory retroactivity principles could constrain that reading.

43. **§§ 2, 3, 5(b)—Fair-notice concerns.** Undefined capability standards and uncertain prohibited activities are especially consequential when violations carry up to ten years’ imprisonment. They create potential vagueness and fair-notice challenges, although clearer applications of the statute might remain enforceable.

### International agreement and duration

44. **§ 6—Negotiation duty does not ensure an agreement.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate,” but need not obtain, bring into force, or secure compliance with an agreement. The provision therefore does not guarantee equivalent foreign restrictions.

45. **§ 6—Deadline and equivalence are unclear.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” could describe a deadline to begin efforts rather than finish negotiations. “Equivalent” also leaves unresolved whether foreign regimes must reproduce § 3’s exemptions and how differences would be evaluated.

46. **§ 7(a)—Required report has no commissioning mechanism.** The bill does not direct anyone to request or fund the National Academies report, prescribe its contents, or set a deadline. Its contemplated early-termination process may therefore never become practically available.

47. **§ 7(a)—Safety finding lacks criteria.** “Can be developed safely” supplies no acceptable-risk standard or indication whether Congress must assess all covered systems or only some class of them. This makes the condition for ending the prohibition uncertain.

48. **§ 7(a)—Joint resolution requires ordinary constitutional enactment.** The reference to Congress finding safety “by joint resolution” does not expressly address presidential presentment. A legally operative joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential approval or a veto override, rather than congressional action alone.

49. **§ 7(a)—Early termination affects only the prohibition.** The provision expressly ends the § 3 prohibition, not the registry or the rest of the Act. The resulting obligations—and treatment of liability for earlier violations—are not explained.

50. **§§ 7(a), 7(b)—Safety-dependent duration is overridden by a fixed sunset.** The entire Act expires ten years after enactment regardless of whether Congress finds covered systems safe. Thus the apparent safety condition does not govern the ultimate duration of the prohibition.

51. **§§ 7(b), 8—Effective operating period is shorter than ten years.** The sunset runs from enactment, but effectiveness starts 180 days later. The Act therefore operates for approximately nine and a half years, not ten years after becoming effective.

52. **§ 7(b)—Post-sunset consequences are not expressly addressed.** “Cease to have effect” does not specify treatment of pending cases, accrued penalties, or outstanding reporting obligations. The general federal saving statute may preserve some liabilities, so sunset should not be assumed to erase earlier violations.
